subject: Behavioral Economics
title: Inequity Aversion
description: A quick win: understand Inequity Aversion.

hook.text: Two monkeys did the same task. One got a grape, the other a cucumber. The cucumber monkey threw it at the researcher.

buildup.text: De Waal's capuchin experiment showed that primates reject unequal rewards. Fairness is wired deeper than rationality.

discovery.text: Fehr and Schmidt modeled inequity aversion. People dislike both getting less than others and getting more than others.

twist.text: Advantageous inequity stings too. Guilt from getting too much drives people to share, donate, and equalize outcomes.

climax.text: Fairness preferences explain wage compression, charitable giving, and progressive taxation. Equity is an economic force.

punchline.text: Even monkeys reject an unfair deal. Humans are no different.

quiz.question: What happened when one monkey received a grape and the other a cucumber?
options: The cucumber monkey rejected its reward and showed anger
The grape monkey shared with the other

details.summary: People dislike unfair outcomes even at personal cost. Inequity aversion means individuals will reject profitable deals if they perceive the distribution as unjust, sacrificing money to punish unfairness or to avoid having more than their fair share.
details.whyItMatters: Inequity aversion constrains market outcomes and shapes labor relations. Workers who perceive pay as unfair reduce effort. Consumers boycott companies they view as unfair. These responses show that fairness is an economic force.
takeaways: People sacrifice personal gain to punish perceived unfairness
Both disadvantageous and advantageous inequity trigger discomfort
Fairness concerns constrain profit-maximizing behavior in markets

faq.question: Why would someone reject free money over fairness?
faq.answer: In ultimatum games, people routinely reject offers of 20 percent or less, preferring zero to accepting an unfair split. The psychological pain of accepting unfair treatment exceeds the utility of the money. Punishing unfairness feels worth the cost.

faq.question: Do people also dislike having more than their fair share?
faq.answer: Yes, though less intensely. Some people experience guilt when they receive disproportionately more. The Fehr-Schmidt model captures this asymmetry: disadvantageous inequity is more aversive than advantageous inequity.
